t: Find Minimum Log Transportation Cost — Simple Math
o: Two logs of lengths n and m must fit on three trucks of capacity k; cutting a piece of length x into a and x−a costs a·(x−a). If both logs already fit (n ≤ k and m ≤ k), cost is 0 (Example 2). Otherwise at least one cut is needed; since a single cut turns one log into two pieces and the other log takes the third truck, exactly one cut suffices whenever the input is feasible. For a log of length L > k we must split it as p and L−p with both parts ≤ k, i.e. p ∈ [L−k, k]; the product p(L−p) is a downward parabola maximized at p = L/2, so it is minimized at the interval endpoints p = L−k, giving cost k·(L−k). Example 1: L=6, k=5 → 5·1 = 5.
k: If both logs fit, answer is 0; otherwise exactly one cut of the longer log is needed
Cutting L into p and L−p with both ≤ k forces p ∈ [L−k, k]
Product p(L−p) is minimized at the boundary p = L−k, yielding cost k(L−k)

a.i: Feasibility guarantees at most one log needs cutting (two cuts would produce four pieces but only three trucks, and the guarantee ensures a valid plan exists). The cheapest legal split of an oversized log of length L puts the smaller piece at L−k and the larger at k, minimizing the product. So the answer is 0 if max(n,m) ≤ k, else k·(max(n,m)−k).

a.n: Approach 2: Brute Force over Split Points
a.i: For small ranges you can enumerate every legal split point p of the longer log and take the minimum product, verifying the logic empirically. It matches the closed form but is mainly useful as a sanity check during a contest.
s: For p from L−k to k, evaluate p·(L−p) and keep the minimum.
a.t: O(k) — scans all legal split points of the longer log.

w: Give the O(1) formula; mention brute force only as verification. Pitfalls: 64-bit output type (k up to 10^5 makes the product up to 10^10, exceeding 32-bit ints), and assuming both logs might need cutting — with three trucks and guaranteed feasibility, one cut always suffices. Follow-ups: minimize the maximum piece instead, more trucks, or multiple logs requiring a greedy/priority assignment.
